To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the BBUG were an important part of the German management education system in the 1950 and 1960s.

the BBUG were a very successful German initiative in the field of advanced top management education, that the BBUG was a unique German phenomenon and that there was no ‘Americanisation’ in this case, at least not in the sense of an imitation of American management education.
the Baden-Baden Talks (BBUG) were not a ‘copy’ of American Management Training (MT).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the BBUG can be understood as a response to the American model of advanced management training.

the question why the BBUG were not a ‘second Harvard Business School’ as some of its proponents hoped for, but a German model for advanced management training that was based on the principles of the German economic miracle and the ‘German way’ of management.
the question of whether the Americanisation of the BBUG was a success story, or whether the German model was more of an alternative.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BBUG did not represent a ‘German’ alternative to the American management training model.
the BBUG was neither American nor European, but German.
the BBUG did not Americanise German management but rather Germanised American management training.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
German managers in the 1950's were very much interested in the American model of top management training, but they did not want to follow it blindly.
the BBUG was a German response to the perceived American challenge to the traditional German management style and to the American lead for management training.
the BBUG was not an example of Americanisation, neither was it an example of the ‘German model’ of management.
The main takeaway from our work is that
German business leaders were not only interested in American management techniques and methods.
the Americanisation of German management was neither a linear process nor was it the result of the import of American management methods.
the BBUG were not the result of a process of Americanisation.
